jesse.text: If you were born as Jesse James, you'd ride with killers at sixteen.
Then you'd rob banks and trains for sixteen years.
Then newspapers would call you a hero.
And the man who finally stops you?
And the war that makes you?
A farm near Kearney, in Clay County, Missouri.
Your father, Robert, is a Baptist preacher.
Your mother, Zerelda, is tall, tough, and afraid of nothing.
Your big brother, four years older.
The farm grows hemp and tobacco.
And your family owns enslaved people.
When you're three, your father rides west to the California gold fields.
He goes to preach to the miners.
Then she marries a quiet country doctor, Reuben Samuel.
You grow up in the fields with Frank.
But Missouri is a border state.
And in eighteen sixty-one, the Civil War comes to your front door.
Then he rides with William Quantrill's guerrillas.
So you stay home and work the field.
Union militia ride onto the farm.
They put a rope around his neck.
And they hang him from a tree.
Then they pull him up again.
Then they find you in the field.
Soon you ride with a man called Bloody Bill Anderson.
That summer, a bullet hits you in the chest.
Bloody Bill's men stop a train.
On board are Union soldiers going home on leave.
Hours later, Union troops ride out after the guerrillas.
More than a hundred of those soldiers die too.
Records say you and Frank are both there.
A month later, Bloody Bill is killed in an ambush.
Then, in the spring of eighteen sixty-five, the war ends.
And a Union patrol shoots you through the lung.
The person who nurses you back?
In Missouri, former rebels can't vote.
They can't even work as lawyers.
And the banks belong to the men who won.
A gang robs a bank in broad daylight.
It's one of the first daytime bank robberies in peacetime America.
Some say you ride with them.
Some say you're still in bed with your wound.
But three years later, there's no doubt.
And you think he's the man who killed Bloody Bill.
Your foot catches in the stirrup.
You escape on the back of Frank's horse.
And that horse leads the law straight to you.
Now your name is in every newspaper.
His name is John Newman Edwards.
He writes about you like a knight.
There's no evidence you ever give anything to the poor.
So you start writing letters to the papers yourself.
Your gang pulls loose a rail.
A train comes around the bend.
It's one of the first train robberies in the American West.
Now you're not just an outlaw.
In eighteen seventy-four, you marry Zee.
The one who saved your life.
So they hire the Pinkerton Detective Agency.
Pinkerton men surround your mother's farmhouse.
They think you and Frank are inside.
They throw a device through the window.
Your little half-brother, Archie, is eight years old.
Your mother's right arm is shattered.
And Missouri turns on the Pinkertons.
Lawmakers nearly pass a bill to forgive you.
Thank you so much for watching, and for asking for this one.
Who should I be born as next?
Drop a name in the comments.
And if you like these stories, a subscribe really helps.
Three of you walk into the First National Bank.
The cashier, Joseph Heywood, says the safe has a time lock.
The door is closed, but not locked.
He's shot dead for that lie.
A medical student fires from a hotel window.
In minutes, two of your men lie dead in the street.
The Youngers are hit again and again.
You ride out with almost nothing.
And for two weeks, hundreds of men hunt you.
The Youngers are cornered in a swamp.
This time, that's what saves you.
You and Zee have a son and a daughter.
For three years, you're almost normal.
Not men who'd die for you.
Now the governor, Thomas Crittenden, makes a promise.
Five thousand dollars each, for you and Frank.
Then he makes a quieter promise.
He grew up reading about you.
A small house on a hill.
You live here as Thomas Howard.
The Ford brothers stay with you.
You take off your gun belt.
You don't want the neighbors to see it.
Then you notice a picture on the wall.
You step onto a chair to fix it.
Your back is to the room.
Some say the picture is a stitched sampler.
Bob Ford runs to send a telegram.
Within days, both Fords are charged with murder.
And the same day, the governor pardons them.
Then the Fords go on stage.
Night after night, they act out your death for paying crowds.
Ten years later, Bob is shot dead in a Colorado saloon.
Six months after your death, he walks into the governor's office.
He lives for thirty-three more years.
He shows strangers around the old family farm.
Your mother puts a stone on your grave.
It calls your killer a traitor and a coward.
And for a hundred years, people whisper.
Maybe it isn't you in that grave.
In nineteen ninety-five, scientists dig you up.
In one, you're a preacher's son in a quiet Missouri field.
In the other, you're the most wanted man in America.
You tip a train off its tracks.
You lose your little brother to a bomb.
And you die standing on a chair, fixing a picture.
Your back to a man you trusted.
Did you ever believe the Robin Hood story?
Or did you just let it sell?
Was Jesse James a rebel, or just a robber?

redbaron.text: If you were born as Manfred von Richthofen, you'd shoot down eighty planes.
Then you'd paint your own plane blood red, so everyone knows who's coming.
Then a bullet would crack your skull in the middle of the sky.
And the man who finally kills you?
Nobody knows, even today.
But right now?
You're a baby.
No plane.
No medals.
No red paint.
And airplanes?
They haven't even been invented yet.
May second, eighteen ninety-two.
You're born Manfred Albrecht von Richthofen.
A baron, near the city of Breslau, in the Kingdom of Prussia.
Today, that city is Wroclaw, in Poland.
Your family is old nobility, and your father is a cavalry officer.
You have an older sister, Ilse.
Then come two little brothers, Lothar and Bolko.
And you love one thing more than anything else.
Hunting.
You shoot birds, deer and wild boar in the forests near home.
You hang the antlers on your bedroom wall, one trophy after another.
Remember that wall.
At eleven, your father sends you away to a military cadet school.
You hate it.
You hate the drills, the rules and the lessons.
The only thing you care about is sport.
You climb, you ride, and you jump anything they put in front of you.
At nineteen, you join a cavalry regiment, the First Uhlans.
Lancers on horseback, in bright uniforms, with long steel lances.
It's the life you always wanted.
For now.
August, nineteen fourteen.
War.
Your regiment rides east against Russia, then west into France and Belgium.
You're twenty-two years old.
On one patrol, French cavalry ambush your troop in a forest.
You only just get away.
And very quickly, you learn something.
Cavalry is finished.
Machine guns, barbed wire, and trenches stretch from the sea to Switzerland.
There's no room left for a man on a horse.
So the army makes you a supply officer, far behind the lines.
You hand out food to soldiers who actually get to fight.
You write an angry letter to your commanders.
You didn't go to war to collect cheese and eggs.
Then you look up at the sky.
Airplanes.
In May, nineteen fifteen, you join the air service.
Not as a pilot, but as an observer.
You sit in the back seat with a map, a camera and a gun.
Then, on a train that October, you meet a man called Oswald Boelcke.
He's already one of Germany's most famous aces.
You ask him his secret.
His answer is simple.
Fly in close, aim well, and the enemy falls.
You decide right there that you'll be a pilot.
Your first solo flight?
You crash it.
In the spring of nineteen sixteen, over Verdun, you finally hit a French plane.
It falls behind enemy lines.
Nobody confirms it, so it doesn't count.
August, nineteen sixteen.
You're on the Russian front, flying a slow two-seat bomber.
Then Boelcke comes east, looking for pilots for a brand new fighter squadron.
Jasta Two.
He knocks on your door, and he picks you.
September seventeenth.
The sky over Cambrai, in France.
You dive on a British two-seater and you fire.
Its propeller stops turning.
It glides down behind German lines.
Your first confirmed kill.
You land in the field right beside it.
Both British airmen are dying.
That night, you write to a jeweler in Berlin.
You order a small silver cup, engraved with the date and the type of plane.
Remember that cup.
Then you order another one.
And another.
October twenty-eighth.
Boelcke chases a British plane, with his friend Erwin Boehme close beside him.
They swerve the same way, and their planes touch.
Boelcke's wing tears away, and he falls.
At his funeral, you carry his medals on a black cushion.
You're twenty-four, and your teacher is gone.
Then, in November, you meet Lanoe Hawker.
He's one of Britain's best, and some call him the British Boelcke.
Round and round you turn, lower and lower.
His fuel runs low.
He breaks away for home.
And you get him.
Victory number eleven.
You take his machine gun and hang it in your room.
January, nineteen seventeen.
Sixteen kills.
Germany gives you the Pour le Merite, Prussia's highest military order.
Pilots call it the Blue Max.
And you get your own squadron, Jasta Eleven.
Then you do something no one else would dare.
You paint your plane bright red.
You want every enemy in the sky to see you coming.
The French call you the Red Devil.
The name Red Baron?
That comes later, mostly after you're gone.
April, nineteen seventeen.
The British call it Bloody April.
They lose hundreds of planes in a single month.
You shoot down more than twenty of them yourself.
Your little brother Lothar joins your squadron.
Now there are two Richthofens hunting in the sky.
Back home, Germany goes crazy for you.
Your face is on postcards and posters.
Fan letters arrive by the sack.
You even write a book about your war, and it sells everywhere.
July sixth, nineteen seventeen.
You lead an attack on a group of British two-seaters.
Then a gunner fires from far away.
A bullet grazes your head and cracks your skull.
You go blind.
Your engine cuts out.
You're falling.
Then your sight comes back, just enough.
You land in a field, covered in blood.
You survive.
But you're not the same man anymore.
You suffer headaches and sickness.
You go back to flying long before your wound is healed.
You're quieter now, and people around you say you've changed.
In your own words, every fight leaves you in a dark mood.
And remember the silver cups?
By your sixtieth victory, Germany is running short of silver.
The jeweler can't make them anymore.
So the cups stop.
The war doesn't.
Quick pause.
Thank you so much for watching, and for asking for this one.
Who should I be born as next?
Drop a name in the comments.
And if you like these stories, a subscribe really helps.
Now, back to the front.
You command a whole fighter wing now.
Four squadrons that move by train and tent along the front.
The Allies call it the Flying Circus.
Your pilots paint their planes in every color.
But only yours is red from nose to tail.
And now you fly a new machine, the Fokker triplane.
Three wings.
It isn't fast, but it turns like nothing else in the sky.
March, nineteen eighteen.
Germany throws everything into one last huge attack.
You keep scoring.
Sixty-five.
Seventy.
April twentieth.
Victory number eighty.
No pilot in the whole war gets more.
Your commanders want you out of the cockpit for good.
A living hero is worth more to them than a dead one.
You keep flying.
April twenty-first, nineteen eighteen.
The very next morning.
High over the Somme valley, your wing meets British planes.
A young Canadian pilot, Wilfrid May, is on his first real patrol.
His guns jam, and he runs.
You chase him.
Low.
Very low, right over the river.
Then over the trenches, where Australian soldiers are waiting.
You're breaking your own rule.
Never follow an enemy down over his own lines.
Behind you, another Canadian, Captain Roy Brown, dives in to help his friend.
On the ground, Australian gunners open fire.
One bullet enters your side and goes up through your chest.
Your triplane comes down hard in a field, almost a landing.
Soldiers run toward it.
You're already dead.
Twenty-five years old.
Gone.
Then the soldiers start cutting pieces off your plane.
The fabric.
The seat.
The guns.
Remember your trophy wall?
Now you're the trophy.
So who fired the shot?
The Royal Air Force gives the kill to Roy Brown.
But the bullet came from below and to the side.
Most historians now believe it was an Australian on the ground.
Which one?
Nobody can say for sure.
The next day, the Australians bury you with full military honors.
Officers carry your coffin, and riflemen fire a salute.
Allied pilots fly over German lines and drop a message.
The Red Baron is dead.
Back home, your mother keeps your room just as you left it.
The antlers.
The silver cups.
Seven months later, Germany loses the war.
Lothar survives it, then dies in a plane crash a few years later.
And even your grave won't rest.
You're moved from France to Berlin, and later to a family grave in Wiesbaden.
Two lives.
In one, you're a cavalry boy with a lance and a bright uniform.
In the other, you're the most famous pilot on Earth.
You learn from the best, and you bury him.
You paint your plane red.
You shoot down eighty planes.
You survive a bullet to the head.
And you die chasing just one more.
Manfred von Richthofen.
Here's the mystery.
More than a hundred years later, nobody can prove who fired that last bullet.
So you tell me.
Who really shot down the Red Baron?

spartacus.text: If you were born as Spartacus, you'd fight to the death for Roman crowds.
Then you'd break out with nothing but kitchen knives.
Then you'd beat army after army of the strongest power on Earth.
And when it all ends?
Six thousand of your people line the road to Rome.
But right now?
You're a baby.
No sword.
No chains.
No army.
And Rome?
It doesn't even know you exist.
Nobody knows the year you're born.
It's somewhere around a hundred years before Christ.
You're born in Thrace.
Today, that land is Bulgaria, with parts of Greece and Turkey.
We don't even know your real name.
Spartacus is simply what the Romans write down.
Your people are horsemen and fighters, living in tribes across the mountains.
The ancient writers say almost nothing about your childhood.
But they agree on one thing.
You're strong, very strong, and you're smart.
One writer, Plutarch, says you're more like a Greek than a Thracian.
From a Roman writer, that's high praise.
There's also a woman from your tribe with you.
A prophetess.
One night, she sees a snake coiled around your face while you sleep.
She says it's a sign of great power.
And of a terrible end.
Remember that snake.
Then Rome comes.
Some writers say you serve in Rome's army as a hired soldier.
Then you desert, and you're caught, and you're sold.
Now you're a slave.
They take one look at your size, and they send you to Capua.
It's a rich city south of Rome, famous for its gladiator schools.
Your owner is a man called Lentulus Batiatus.
He trains you to die well, for other people's fun.
You fight as a Thracian, with a curved sword and a small shield.
You sleep locked in a cell.
You eat barley porridge to build muscle.
Romans even call gladiators barley men.
You watch your friends die on the sand, one after another.
And you start whispering.
About two hundred men plan an escape together.
Then someone talks.
The plot is discovered.
Seventy-three years before Christ.
You don't wait to be punished.
About seventy of you rush the kitchen.
You grab cleavers, meat spits and knives.
And you fight your way out into the street.
On the road, you find wagons full of gladiator weapons.
Now you're armed.
You climb Mount Vesuvius.
Yes, that Vesuvius, long before it buries Pompeii.
You choose three leaders.
You, and two Gauls, Crixus and Oenomaus.
Rome laughs at a few runaway slaves.
They send a praetor, Gaius Claudius Glaber, with three thousand men.
He doesn't even bother to attack.
He blocks the only path down the mountain.
He'll just starve you out.
But the cliffs are covered in wild vines.
You cut them, and you twist them into ladders.
At night, you climb down the cliffs, one by one.
Then you circle all the way around the Roman camp.
And you attack it from behind.
Glaber's men run for their lives.
You win.
Now slaves start running to you from all over the south.
Farm workers.
Shepherds.
Herdsmen.
Thousands, then tens of thousands.
Rome sends another praetor, Publius Varinius.
One of his officers, Cossinius, is bathing in a spring when you attack.
He barely escapes half naked.
Days later, you catch him again, and this time he dies.
Varinius tries to trap you in your camp.
So one night, you tie dead bodies upright at the gates.
You keep the campfires burning.
And your whole army slips away in the dark.
Then you beat Varinius in open battle.
You even capture his own horse.
Remember the prophetess?
Great power.
It's coming true.
The ancient writers say you soon lead seventy thousand people.
Some say many more.
Nobody really counted.
And you try to keep it fair.
Appian, another ancient writer, says you share the loot equally.
You ban traders from bringing gold or silver into your camp.
Only iron and bronze, to make more weapons.
But your army is not one army.
Crixus wants to stay in Italy and plunder.
You want to march north, over the Alps, and go home.
The sources don't agree on why.
But you split.
Seventy-two years before Christ.
Now Rome sends both of its consuls, with two full armies.
Crixus marches off with thirty thousand men.
Near Mount Garganus, a Roman army catches them.
Crixus dies, and most of his men die with him.
You beat one consul.
Then you beat the other.
And then, Appian says, you do something terrible.
You make three hundred Roman prisoners fight each other to the death.
To honor Crixus.
As gladiators, just like you were.
Quick pause.
Thank you so much for watching, and for asking for this one.
Who should I be born as next?
Drop a name in the comments.
And if you like these stories, a subscribe really helps.
Now, back to Italy.
You march north, the whole length of Italy.
All the way to Mutina, near the foot of the Alps.
The local governor attacks you with ten thousand men.
You crush him.
The mountains are right there.
Freedom is right there.
And then?
You turn around.
Why?
Nobody knows.
Maybe your people don't want to leave the rich farms of Italy.
Maybe some of them dream of taking Rome itself.
The ancient writers simply can't agree.
Rome is terrified now.
Nobody wants the command.
Except one man.
Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome.
He raises new legions with his own money.
When some of his men run from you, he brings back an old punishment.
Decimation.
One soldier in every ten is chosen by lot.
Then his own comrades beat him to death.
Now his men fear Crassus more than they fear you.
You head south, to the very toe of Italy.
You make a deal with Cilician pirates.
They'll ship your army across the water to Sicily.
You pay them.
They sail away.
They never come back.
Then Crassus does something nobody expects.
His men dig a trench right across the land, from sea to sea.
They build a wall behind it.
You're trapped.
Winter comes.
One snowy night, you fill part of the trench with earth and branches.
And you break through with a third of your army.
Seventy-one years before Christ.
Rome calls its great general Pompey home from Spain.
Another army lands in the south.
Roman legions are closing in from every side.
Part of your army breaks away again, and Crassus wipes it out.
And Crassus wants the glory before Pompey can steal it.
Appian says you crucify one Roman prisoner between the two camps.
You want your men to see what waits for them if they lose.
Near the river Silarus, you face Crassus at last.
Before the battle, your men bring you your horse.
You draw your sword.
And you kill it.
Plutarch says you tell them why.
If you win, you'll have plenty of horses.
If you lose, you won't need one.
Then you go on foot, straight toward Crassus.
You cut through the crowd.
You kill two centurions.
Then you're surrounded.
And you go down fighting.
Your body is never found.
Remember the snake?
Great power, and a terrible end.
Here it is.
Six thousand survivors are captured.
Crassus crucifies them along the Appian Way.
From Capua, all the way to Rome.
Then Pompey arrives.
He catches five thousand more who ran north.
And he tells the Senate that he ended the war.
Crassus never forgives him.
Two thousand years later, your name is still a word for rebellion.
Two lives.
In one, you're a Thracian with a name nobody remembers.
In the other, you're the slave who makes Rome shake.
You break out with kitchen knives.
You climb down a volcano on vines.
You beat two praetors and two consuls.
You reach the Alps, and you turn back.
And you die on foot, sword in hand.
Spartacus.
Here's the question nobody can answer.
At the Alps, freedom is one march away.
So you tell me.
Why do you think Spartacus turned back?

sherlock.text: If you were born as Sherlock Holmes, you'd solve crimes Scotland Yard can't even understand.
Then you'd meet the one man as brilliant as you.
And he'd be a criminal.
Then you'd go over a waterfall in Switzerland.
And three years later?
You walk back into your own living room.
But right now?
You're a baby.
No pipe.
No violin.
No Watson.
And the scariest thing in your life?
Boredom.
You'll hate it forever.
Remember that.
Around eighteen fifty-four.
You're born Sherlock Holmes.
Quick truth.
You're not a real person.
You live inside the stories of Arthur Conan Doyle.
And those stories say very little about your childhood.
So everything here comes from what you say yourself, inside the books.
Your family are country squires, quiet landowners somewhere in England.
But your grandmother is the sister of a famous French painter.
Art in the blood, you say, can take very strange forms.
You have one brother, Mycroft, seven years older than you.
And he's even smarter than you are.
You admit it openly.
But Mycroft is lazy.
He'd rather sit in his quiet club all day than chase anything.
Remember Mycroft.
You go to college for two years.
You don't make friends.
You stay in your room, inventing your own little methods of thinking.
Then one morning, on your way to chapel, a dog bites your ankle.
A bull terrier.
You're stuck in bed for ten days.
Your only visitor is the dog's owner, Victor Trevor.
He becomes your only friend.
He invites you to his father's house in Norfolk for the holidays.
And there, at dinner, you read the old man like a book.
You tell him he's been a boxer.
You tell him he's done a lot of digging.
Then you tell him he once knew someone with the initials J.A.
And that he tried very hard to forget them.
The old man faints on the spot.
When he wakes up, he tells you something.
Make this your profession.
Remember that dinner.
That's where your real life begins.
You move to London.
You take rooms in a small street near the British Museum.
You study anything that might help you catch a criminal.
Chemistry.
Anatomy.
Poisons.
Mud from every part of London.
You write a paper on a hundred and forty kinds of tobacco ash.
And you learn nothing that won't help.
You don't even know the Earth goes around the Sun.
And you don't care.
Your brain is an attic, you say.
Fill it with junk, and the useful things get lost.
Eighteen eighty-one.
Saint Bartholomew's Hospital.
You're alone in a chemistry lab, testing blood.
A friend walks in with a stranger.
A thin, sunburnt army doctor with a wounded shoulder.
You shake his hand.
And you calmly tell him he's just come back from Afghanistan.
He's stunned.
His name is John Watson.
You both need cheap rooms, so you share.
Two twenty-one B, Baker Street.
Seventeen steps up to the sitting room.
A patient landlady, Mrs. Hudson.
A violin you bought from a pawnbroker for almost nothing.
Chemicals all over the table.
And bullet holes in the wall.
You shoot the Queen's initials into it.
Indoors.
Watson thinks you're mad.
Then the police start knocking at your door.
Inspector Lestrade.
Inspector Gregson.
They're completely stuck.
You're the world's only consulting detective.
They come to you whenever they're lost.
Your first big case together?
A dead man in an empty house.
And one word written on the wall in blood.
Rache.
German for revenge.
You solve it in days.
Then Watson writes it up, and he calls it A Study in Scarlet.
Now the whole public knows your name.
But there's another side of you.
When there's no case, you sink.
You lie on the sofa for days, and you barely speak.
You play strange music on your violin in the middle of the night.
Remember the boredom?
That's it.
For you, a puzzle isn't a job.
It's air.
So you hire London's street boys as your spies.
The Baker Street Irregulars, at a shilling a day.
Eighteen eighty-eight.
A king hires you.
He wants a photograph back from a woman.
Irene Adler, an opera singer.
You disguise yourself as a priest and fake an accident outside her house.
You trick her into showing you where she hides the photo.
You win.
Or so you think.
The next morning, she's gone.
She saw right through your disguise.
She leaves a letter for you.
And a photograph of herself.
You keep it.
From then on, she's simply the woman.
You lose only a few times in your whole life.
This is the one you never forget.
Quick pause.
Thank you so much for watching, and for asking for this one.
Who should I be born as next?
Drop a name in the comments.
And if you like these stories, a subscribe really helps.
Now, back to Baker Street.
Watson marries and moves out.
But the cases keep coming.
A woman whose sister dies whispering about a speckled band.
A deadly snake, sent through a vent in the wall.
Then a family on Dartmoor, haunted by the legend of a giant hound.
A man found dead, with huge paw prints beside his body.
Everyone says it's a curse.
You say it's a man.
And you're right.
By eighteen ninety-one, you've found something bigger.
Behind half the crimes in London, there's one mind.
Professor James Moriarty.
A math genius and a respected professor.
And the center of a criminal web across the whole city.
You call him the Napoleon of crime.
You start cutting his threads, one by one.
He walks into Baker Street himself.
He tells you to stop.
You don't.
Then the attacks start.
A carriage nearly runs you down.
A brick falls from a roof.
A man jumps you with a club.
Your rooms are set on fire.
So you flee to Europe with Watson.
May, eighteen ninety-one.
Switzerland.
The Reichenbach Falls.
A boy runs up with a message.
Watson is needed back at the hotel.
It's a trick.
Now you're alone on the narrow path.
And Moriarty walks up.
He lets you write a short note.
Then you fight at the very edge.
Watson runs back.
He finds your walking stick, and your note.
Two sets of footprints going to the edge.
None coming back.
Gone.
Except you're not.
You use a Japanese wrestling trick.
Moriarty goes over.
You don't.
You climb the rock wall and hide.
Because one of Moriarty's men is still watching from above.
So you let the world think you're dead.
Even Watson.
Only one person knows the truth.
Remember Mycroft?
Lazy Mycroft.
He quietly sends you money for three years.
You travel through Tibet, Persia, and the deserts of Arabia.
You go by a Norwegian name, Sigerson.
Eighteen ninety-four.
Watson is back home in London.
An old book seller bumps into him on the street.
Minutes later, the old man is standing in Watson's study.
He straightens up.
It's you.
Watson faints.
The only time in his life.
That same night, you catch Moriarty's last dangerous man.
Colonel Sebastian Moran.
He's been waiting with an air gun to shoot you through your own window.
He hits a wax bust of you instead.
You work for another ten years.
Then, one day, you just stop.
You retire to a small farm on the Sussex Downs, near the sea.
And you keep bees.
Bees.
You even write a whole book about them.
Then, in nineteen fourteen, war is coming.
